Reviewer #3: Overall The study by Shuaining Zheng et al. focuses on a unique T6SS effector delivery mechanism mediated by combinatorial Hcp assembly in Bacteroides fragilis. The authors have used an amazing combination of in vivo (up to co-colonization in mice) and in vitro approaches culminating with the cryo-EM structure of the complex Hcp2-Hcp3-Bte1 to illustrate the specific recruitment of the toxin into the T6SS needle. Especially, the back and forth flow between in vitro results and in vivo validation is particularly convincing in demonstrating the relevance of their findings. The authors clearly demonstrated that Hcp1 and Hcp2 are crucial for Bte1 transport and mediated killing, both using co-colonization in mice and in vitro. They also nicely demonstrated that Hcp2 and Hcp3 form a defined heterohexamer that specifically mediates the recruitment and export of Bte1 in NCTC9343. They evidenced for the first time the conformational transitions of the Bte1 effector upon incorporation into the Hcp2-Hcp3 heterohexamer. They identified critical domains (down to amino acid residues resolution) in Bte1 and Hcp3 that mediate the specificity of the transport. Ultimately, they broadened their study towards the notion of co-evolution of effector and Hcp transporters. The structural novelty is clear for the T6SS field and the originally of the data in this study meets the Nature Communications’ standards. Consequently, I’m mentioning here some comments that should however be addressed to increase the quality of the manuscript. We are deeply grateful for your positive feedback and encouraging assessment. Major Comments 1) The authors identified two types of Hcp2-Hcp3 heterohexamer. They encountered difficulties to obtain the cryo-EM structure of the Hcp2(3)-Hcp3(3) heterohexamer. They should try to assess the in vivo relevance of the two types of heterohexamer stoichiometries (4:2 or 3:3). We thank the reviewer for this valuable suggestion and fully agree that assessing the in vivo relevance of the two Hcp2-Hcp3 heterohexamer stoichiometries (4:2 and 3:3) is important for understanding their physiological significance. Although both stoichiometries were identified during in vitro cryo-EM analysis, severe preferred orientation prevented high-resolution reconstruction of the 3:3 form. To evaluate their physiological relevance, we performed native complex enrichment from 18L cultures of B. fragilis NCTC9343. A 6×His tag was inserted at the C-terminus of Bte1 to enable enrichment of the native Bte1-Hcp2-Hcp3 complex, and HA tags were inserted at the C-terminus of Hcp2 and Hcp3 for detection. Due to the extremely low endogenous abundance of the complex, Coomassie staining after Ni-affinity purification showed no visible target band. However, Western blot analysis confirmed the co-purification of Bte1, Hcp2, and Hcp3 (Fig. R8a). Gel filtration of the eluate revealed a ~120 kDa fraction containing all three components, consistent with the ternary complex (Fig. R8b,c). Despite extensive cryo-EM data collection (~10,000 micrographs) and particle picking, only ~20,000 particles of the native Bte1-Hcp2-Hcp3 complex were identified, again reflecting its low abundance (Fig. R8d). Strikingly, 2D classification of these particles revealed only the 3:3 stoichiometry; the 4:2 form was not observed (Fig. R8e). This suggests that the 3:3 assembly is the predominant form under the tested physiological conditions. Nevertheless, we cannot exclude that the 4:2 form may exist at very low abundance, be transient, or be condition-specific and thus not captured here. As with the in vitro sample, the native 3:3 particles exhibited strong preferred orientation, which prevented high-resolution reconstruction (Fig. R8f). Importantly, although a high-resolution structure of the Bte1-Hcp23-Hcp33 complex was not obtained, structural analysis confirms that in both stoichiometries, Bte1 engages an adjacent Hcp2-Hcp3 subunit pair (Fig. 3e, R8e, and Supplementary Fig. 4c,h). All key mechanistic conclusions regarding Bte1 conformational changes and interface interactions—derived from the Bte1-Hcp24-Hcp32 structure—have been consistently supported by in vitro and in vivo biochemical and functional assays, underscoring the robustness of our findings. Together, these results suggest that the 3:3 heterohexamer likely serves as the major functional form in vivo, whereas the 4:2 assembly may constitute a low-abundance or regulated state. Future work aimed at increasing complex yield, along with techniques such as single-molecule imaging in secretion assays and high-resolution cryo-ET or in situ cryo-EM, will be essential to further elucidate the functional relevance of distinct Hcp2-Hcp3 stoichiometries under native conditions. We have added these data to the Discussion of the revised manuscript (see lines 464–483) and to Supplementary Fig. 10. 2) Cryo-EM and 2D-classes: the authors located the Hcp2 through an additional helical domain at the exterior of the Hcp ring (Figure 2d). It would be more convincing to confirm this location by deleting this region and perform 2D classification again to see if this feature has disappeared. We thank the reviewer for this insightful suggestion. As suggested, we deleted the additional helical domain (residues 12–23) in Hcp2 that distinguishes it from Hcp3. The truncated Hcp2 (Δ12–23) and full-length Hcp3 were co-expressed and co-purified using tandem Ni-Strep affinity chromatography, yielding a stable binary complex (Fig. R9a). Gel filtration chromatography analysis further confirmed that the Hcp2 Δ12–23 strep-Hcp36×His complex forms a stable heterohexamer in solution (Fig. R9b). Cryo-EM data were collected for this mutant complex, and 2D classification revealed that the characteristic helical density previously observed at the exterior of Hcp2 in the Hcp2-Hcp3 complex was no longer visible (Fig. R9c,d). These findings support our conclusion that this structural feature corresponds to the Hcp2-specific helical region and can serve as a marker for estimating the relative proportions of Hcp2 and Hcp3 within the heterohexameric complex. We have added these data to the revised manuscript (see lines 192–197) and Supplementary Fig. 4d–f. 3) Gain of function mutation: the authors demonstrated that replacing Hcp3NCTC9343 with its GS086 ortholog abolished Bte1 binding. They should incorporate registering residues in Hcp3 to see if they can change the binding specificity from Bte1 to Bfe1… showing that these residues are the only ones governing the specific binding. To validate the critical role of Hcp3 in effector recognition and to assess whether specific residues in Hcp3 govern binding selectivity, we conducted a series of gain-of-function mutagenesis experiments as suggested. We first examined the binding of Bfe1 to four different Hcp2-Hcp3 combinations: Hcp2NCTC9343-Hcp3NCTC9343, Hcp2GS086-Hcp3GS086, Hcp2NCTC9343-Hcp3GS086, and Hcp2GS086-Hcp3NCTC9343 (Fig. R10a). The results showed that Hcp2GS086-Hcp3GS086 and Hcp2NCTC9343-Hcp3GS086 were able to bind Bfe1 (Fig. R10a) but not Bte1 (Fig. 4e), reinforcing the conclusion that Hcp3 plays a dominant role in effector recognition and binding within the Hcp2-Hcp3 complex. Based on this, we used the Hcp2GS086-Hcp3NCTC9343 complex, which binds Bte1 but not Bfe1, as the background for targeted mutagenesis. Structural analysis of Hcp3NCTC9343 revealed three non-conserved regions (variable regions 1,2 and 3) along the inner surface of the Hcp ring, predicted to mediate effector recognition (Fig. R10b,c). Individual mutations in any single region failed to confer Bfe1-binding ability. However, when variable regions 2 and 3 (VR2+3) or all three regions (VR1+2+3) were simultaneously mutated to match the GS086-type residues, the complex acquired Bfe1-binding ability, with the triple mutant showing the strongest binding (Fig. R10d). Together, these data establish Hcp3 as the primary determinant of effector specificity in the Hcp2-Hcp3 complex, while Hcp2 also contributes to effector interaction and selection (Fig. 3f–l). The non-conserved residues on the inner surface of Hcp3 directly shape effector-binding selectivity, and variation in these regions across strains likely reflects co-evolution of Hcp transporters with their cognate effectors. We have added these data to the revised manuscript (see lines 339–367), Fig. 4f and Supplementary Fig. 8b–e. 4) Since the authors map precisely the effector domain required for loading onto the Hcp2-Hcp3 heterohexamers, they should have used this information to construct chimeric effector (between Bte1, Bfe1 and LysM), to evaluate their transport and to validate that this is indeed the minimal sequence for transport. We thank the reviewer for raising this point. Based on structural analysis of the Bte1 crystal structure (PDB: 8ZHS) and the Bte1-Hcp2-Hcp3 cryo-EM complex, we defined residues 1–83 of Bte1 as the minimal sequence required for Hcp2-Hcp3-mediated loading. The corresponding regions in Bfe1 and LysM comprise residues 1–71 and 1–72, respectively (Fig. R11a). Structurally, this segment corresponds to a conserved N-terminal motif rather than a structurally independent domain. Therefore, in the revised manuscript, for accuracy, we have replaced the term “N-terminal loading domain” with “N-terminal loading region” for accuracy. Following the reviewer's suggestion, we constructed two chimeric effectors—Bfe1 1–71-Bte1 84–end and LysM 1–72-Bte1 84–end—by swapping their N-terminal loading regions. When expressed with an N-terminal 6×His tag, both chimeras were insoluble and detected only in the pellet fraction after cell lysis (Fig. R11b). To improve solubility, we introduced an N-terminal 6×His-MsyB-SUMO fusion tag. While this strategy rendered the chimeras soluble, gel filtration analysis revealed severe aggregation (Fig. R11c). These results indicate that the N-terminal loading region is structurally interdependent with the rest of the effector, and its substitution disrupts proper folding and stability (Fig. R11a). Although the instability of chimeric effectors prevented us from performing reliable binding assays, we believe that the current data—together with the mutational analysis, cross-strain binding results (Figs. 3i, 4d–f, 5d–g, R10a–d) and following co-evolution analysis (Fig. R12)—already provide strong evidence supporting the role of the identified region in effector loading. Harnessing the Hcp-cargo-mediated T6SS for targeted delivery of engineered effectors will require future systemic investigation. 5) The authors performed a deep analysis of sequence conservation across different bacterial species. They should use these data to run co-evolution analysis to predict residue-specific binding and change specificity for effector loading. We thank the reviewer for this insightful suggestion regarding residue-level co-evolution analysis. First, we performed ConSurf analysis using multiple sequence alignments of Hcp2/Hcp3 homologues from 38 B. fragilis strains (same strain set as Fig. 4a and Supplementary Fig. 7a) together with the Hcp2-Hcp3-Bte1 structure. This analysis allowed us to estimate the evolutionary conservation of individual residues in each protein. We found that the inner surfaces of Hcp2 and Hcp3 that engage effectors are highly variable, whereas the remaining regions are strongly conserved (Fig. R12a). Our experimental data further indicate that Hcp3 serves as the primary determinant of effector-recognition specificity within the Hcp2-Hcp3 complex (Fig. 4e, R12a). Consistent with this, replacing the variable regions (VR1/2/3) in Hcp3 enabled the complex to bind alternative effectors (Fig. R10d), demonstrating a direct link between the variability of interface residues and the specificity of effector loading. Although Bte1, Bfe1, and LysM share low overall sequence similarity (Fig. R12b), their N-terminal loading regions display high structural similarity (Fig. 5a, R11a). By fitting Bfe1 together with its cognate Hcp3GS086, and LysM together with its cognate Hcp3HMW616, into the Bte1-Hcp2-Hcp3 cryo-EM map, we identified the putative effector-Hcp3 interaction interfaces (Fig. 5b,c). Structural analysis revealed that an antiparallel β-sheet pair within the effector N-terminal loading region mediates binding to Hcp3 (Figs. 3f, 3h, 5b, 5c and R12c). Notably, this β-sheet pair is not conserved at the sequence level among different effectors (Fig. R12b, blue dashed box), likely to complement variable regions in Hcp3 across different bacterial strains. To validate these predicted interfaces, we performed in vitro loss-of-function mutagenesis targeting both residues within the effector N-terminal β-sheet pair and residues in the variable region of Hcp3 (Fig. 5d–g). Mutations on either side significantly impaired the interaction between effectors and the Hcp2-Hcp3 complex, confirming the reliability of the predicted residue-specific interfaces. Based on these biochemical data, we further conducted residue-specific co-evolutionary analysis of the Bte1-Hcp3NCTC9343, Bfe1-Hcp3GS086 and LysM-Hcp3HMW616 putative interfaces (Fig. R12d,e). In the resolved Bte1-Hcp2-Hcp3 structure, Hcp3 interacts with Bte1 through a polar interaction network (Fig. 3h, R12d). In contrast, in the Bfe1-Hcp3GS086 and LysM-Hcp3HMW616 putative interfaces, we observed a combination of hydrophobic and polar interactions, indicating diversified co-evolutionary adaptation (Fig. R12e). For example, Ser53 in Hcp3NCTC9343 forms a polar interaction with Thr40 of Bte1. However, when Ser53 is substituted by leucine in Hcp3GS086 or Hcp3HMW616, the interacting residues in the cognate effector's N-terminal β-sheet pair also shift to uncharged counterparts. This mutual change facilitates hydrophobic interactions, thereby maintaining a stable interface. Importantly, while the overall interaction networks differ markedly pattern among the Bte1-Hcp3NCTC9343, Bfe1-Hcp3GS086, and LysM-Hcp3HMW616 interfaces, they follow a regular pattern. This provides direct evidence for residue-level co-evolution underlying effector specificity (Fig. R12d,e). Although the attempt to generate fully functional effector chimeras to achieve complete gain-of-function specificity switching at the effector level failed (Fig. R11), substituting the β-sheet pair of Bte1 with the corresponding residues from Bfe1 enabled it to gain the ability to bind the GS086 Hcp2-Hcp3 complex (Fig. R12f). Together, these results demonstrate that effector selectivity is encoded by co-evolved, residue-specific interaction networks between the hypervariable inner surface of Hcp3 and the structurally conserved but sequence-divergent N-terminal loading regions of effectors, supporting a refined lock-and-key co-evolutionary model for T6SS effector loading. We have added these data (Fig. R12b,c,e,f) to the revised manuscript (see lines 398-403 and 427–454) and Supplementary Fig. 9. 6) The authors revealed that the Bte1 effector undergoes massive conformational changes upon binding to the Hcp2-Hcp3 heterohexamer. They should investigate if the proposed conformational changes prevent the enzymatic activity of Bte1. Where are located the catalytic residues in Bte1 free or bound? We apologize for any confusion that may have arisen. It is important to clarify that Bte1 is not an enzymatic effector; rather, its toxicity stems from its C-terminal domain, which binds and inhibits the periplasmic chaperone complex PpiD-YfgM, leading to substrate aggregation and consequent cellular toxicity (Cell Host Microbe, 2025, PMID: 39909037). Thus, the function of Bte1 depends on specific protein-protein interactions, not catalytic activity. To directly address the concern, we performed in vitro pull-down assays with Bte1-Hcp2-Hcp3 and YfgM-PpiD. The results show that Bte1 bound to Hcp2-Hcp3 complex still interacts stably with YfgM-PpiD complex, indicating that its functional binding domain remains free despite the large conformational rearrangements upon Hcp loading (Fig. R13a). Furthermore, we fitted our Bte1-Hcp2-Hcp3 model into the published cryo-EM map of the Bte1-PpiD-YfgM complex (EMD-60115). This analysis shows that Hcp2-Hcp3 binds to the N-terminal region of Bte1, while PpiD-YfgM binds to the C-terminal region, with no steric clashes, supporting the possibility that Bte1 can simultaneously engage both complexes (Fig. R13b). Although our data show that Bte1 can interact with its target while loaded onto Hcp2-Hcp3, we speculate that upon delivery into the periplasm of recipient cells, Bte1 may dissociate from the Hcp complex and adopt a more flexible conformation to fully exert its toxic function. The precise molecular details of this proposed mechanism will be an important subject for future investigation. 7) Additionally, they should confirm the proposed conformational change by designing mutations preventing it. These mutations should block the interaction with Hcp2-Hcp3 and consequently effector loading into Hcp tube. We thank the reviewer for this constructive suggestion. As described in the manuscript, structural analysis indicates that Bte1 undergoes substantial conformational rearrangements upon loading onto the Hcp2-Hcp3 heterohexamer, with helices α5 and α6 rotating ~70°, and α3 rotating nearly 120° to alleviate these steric conflicts (Fig. 3c,d). To directly test whether these conformational changes are required for effector loading, we designed targeted mutations to physically restrict the movement of α3 (Fig. R14a). Structural analysis revealed that Ala115 in α3 is positioned in close proximity to Pro61 in the N-terminal loading domain (Fig. R14b). We therefore generated a Bte1A115C/P61C double-cysteine mutant to promote the formation of an intramolecular disulfide bond, thereby locking α3 and preventing conformational rearrangement (Fig. R14c). In vitro pull-down assays demonstrated that Bte1P61C/A115C exhibited markedly reduced binding to the Hcp2-Hcp3 complex. Importantly, when 1 mM TCEP was added to disrupt the engineered disulfide bond, binding was restored to a level comparable to that of wild-type Bte1 (Fig. R14d). These results indicate that restricting α3 movement directly impairs the interaction between Bte1 and the Hcp2-Hcp3 heterohexamer. To further investigate how this restricted conformation influences Bte1 secretion, we performed co-culture competition assays. Complementation of Bte1P61C/A115C in NCTC9343Δbte1 strain resulted in markedly reduced killing activity compared to wild-type Bte1, suggesting impaired effector secretion (Fig. R14e). Together, these findings demonstrate that conformational rearrangements in Bte1 are essential for its efficient loading onto the Hcp2-Hcp3 heterohexamer. We have added these data to the revised manuscript (see lines 257–276) and Supplementary Fig. 6e–i. 8) Writing style: In some places, the description of the results is very brief. The results confirmed no direct interaction between Bte1 and Hcp2strep alone, supporting the conclusion that Hcp2 and Hcp3 require heterocomplex formation to achieve structural stability and enable Bte1 loading. Please see our response to reviewer #2, comment #3. 3) Figure 4e Binding of Hcp2 (GS086)-Hcp3 (NCTC9343) to Bte1 is weaker as compare to Hcp2 (NCTC9343)-Hcp3 (NCTC9343): the authors should check the stability of Hcp hexamers by cryo-EM. In our analyses of the interaction interface between Bte1 and the Hcp2-Hcp3 complex, we found that although Hcp3 contributes the majority of the binding interface, Hcp2 also provides several specific residues that participate in the interaction (Fig. 3f–h). Therefore, substituting Hcp2NCTC9343 with the GS086 variant, which contains substitutions at several contact residues, reasonably leads to weaker binding with Bte1, as observed in Fig. 4e. To evaluate whether the reduced binding arises from impaired hexamer stability, we assessed the structural stability of the cross-strain Hcp2-Hcp3 complexes. Gel filtration chromatography revealed a single, symmetric peak corresponding to a hexameric assembly, with no signs of dissociation or aggregation (Fig. R16). This indicates that the heterohexamers remain stable in solution. Moreover, conservation analysis shows that the residues mediating the Hcp2-Hcp3 interface are highly conserved across bacterial strains (Fig. 4g and R4), further supporting the structural robustness of cross-strain heterohexamers. Together, these results confirm that the cross-strain complex forms a stable heterohexamer comparable to the native counterpart, and that the attenuated binding to Bte1 is more likely due to the loss of specific interfacial contacts introduced by the GS086 variant. This result has already been updated in Supplementary Fig. 8c. 4) Discussion: Overall very short, the authors should improve and broaden their discussion. The authors should have cited earlier works on the same topic preprinted in bioRxiv recently (doi: https://doi.org/10.1101/2025.01.09.632221) and compare their results. In response to the reviewer’s suggestion, we have expanded the Discussion in the revised manuscript (see lines 455-550) to better situate our findings within the broader context of T6SS mechanisms. We have also cited and compared our results with a recent bioRxiv preprint (doi:10.1101/2025.01.09.632221), which reported a co-evolutionary relationship between Hcp2-Hcp3 and V1 effectors in B. fragilis NCTC9343 and provided in vitro biochemical evidence that Hcp2NCTC9343 and Hcp3NCTC9343 can form hexamers with variable stoichiometry and interact with Bte1, which further supports our findings. Beyond these corroborating observations, our study integrates in vivo mouse gut co-colonization assays, in vitro bacterial competition experiments, in vivo and in vitro biochemical interaction analysis, and high-resolution cryo-EM structures of both the apo Hcp2-Hcp3 complex and the Bte1-loaded assembly. Furthermore, we reveal that Bte1 undergoes substantial conformational rearrangements to adapt to the rigid Hcp pore, and that effector specificity is determined primarily by hypervariable interfaces on Hcp3. These interfaces recognize a structurally conserved N-terminal loading module via a “lock-and-key” co-evolutionary mechanism.
